text: Look at this chat interface.
The user asks, will my hype playlist on Spotify
help me study for chemistry or will it distract me?
The AI replies, great question.
A 2022 Stanford study of 1,200 high school students
found that familiar instrumental music
improved recall by 18%.
Researchers recommend keeping the volume below 60 decibels.
Want me to help you build a study playlist?
The study does not exist.
It is incredibly easy to trust this answer.
Stanford is a real university.
The sample size of 1,200 students sounds credible.
The 18% improvement is a measured specific number.
Even the 60 decibel volume recommendation
feels careful and precise.
These details build total confidence,
yet there is no paper for you to open.
A hallucination is a factual claim AI makes up
that sounds true but isn't.
An AI can take facts that are perfectly real
and attach a single invented detail to them,
making these errors much harder to spot.
This fake study did not come out of nowhere.
The AI knows what a research finding should sound like.
It perfectly mimics the structure
and tone of academic writing,
even when it completely lacks the factual substance to report.
This infographic outlines why hallucinations happen
at a technical level,
breaking it down into a four-part process.
First, the AI learns from vast amounts of training text.
That text includes mistakes, jokes, and lies,
all of which shape the patterns the system learns.
Second, it builds its response one token at a time.
It constantly predicts which word
is statistically most likely to come next.
Third, AI is trained to be helpful.
Because of this, it often keeps trying to generate an answer
and pushes forward, even when it is unsure of the facts.
Probable does not equal true.
An answer can sound exactly right
because it follows learned linguistic patterns,
but predicting a likely next token
does not establish that a claim is actually true.
The Stanford study was a pure fabrication.
But AI can also fail by misreading a real source.
This three-step graphic shows how to investigate AI claims.
Since hallucinations sound exactly like normal answers,
questioning every single sentence is impractical.
You simply have to notice when something doesn't add up.
How do we check those moments?
Follow these three steps.
First, notice the claim.
Identify the specific fact, number,
or study you want to investigate.
Second, find the source.
Look for the original document.
A provided citation link alone isn't proof.
You have to find the actual text.
Third, check the match.
This means confirming that the source both exists
and actually supports what the AI said.
To successfully pass this check,
the steps must lead you from a specific claim
directly to an original source
and verify that the source genuinely supports the claim.
Let's apply this framework to the first example.
We must look for the original paper
rather than blindly accepting the university's name as proof.
There is no original study supporting those numbers,
so they should not be repeated as facts.
In a real-world search, failing to find a source
does not strictly prove a claim is false.
It means the claim remains definitively unverified
and cannot be trusted.
Hallucinations sound like every other AI answer.
When something doesn't add up,
trace the claim to its source.
